description: We are The Land Alchemists, a two-member team passionate about soil health, regenerative agriculture, climate science and Environmental and Intergenerational Ethics. Our project, YETOS 2050 — Same Rain. Different Soil., uses NASA climate data and Irish soil research to explore how soils respond differently to extreme rainfall, drought, and water scarcity. Inspired by Storm Daniel in Greece, we value scientific integrity and intergenerational ethics. Our team is complete and not recruiting.
summary:
YETOS 2050 is a human-led, NASA-powered agricultural decision-support prototype developed by The Land Alchemists.

Using NASA POWER historical weather data, an illustrative soil-water balance and NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections, it helps farmers explore how different soils and water-management assumptions respond to the same environmental conditions.

Our interactive Streamlit application compares hypothetical irrigation interruption, extreme rainfall and prolonged dry-period scenarios, while giving farmers control over their priorities.

A separate Climate 2050 Lens explores one simulated future year without presenting it as a weather forecast.

Inspired by environmental and intergenerational responsibility, YETOS 2050 makes scientific uncertainty visible rather than hiding it. It does not replace farmer judgment or provide field-validated predictions.

Same Rain. Different Soil. Different Futures.
details:
YETOS 2050 — Same Rain. Different Soil.

The problem

A farmer cannot control the rain, but the same rainfall can produce different outcomes depending on soil characteristics, available water and management choices.

YETOS 2050 explores a central question: How can farmers compare water-related risks without confusing model assumptions with scientific certainty?

Our solution

The Land Alchemists developed YETOS 2050, an interactive, human-led agricultural decision-support prototype using Python and Streamlit.

The application combines:

  • NASA POWER: Historical daily meteorological data for the Limerick, Ireland, study area, using 2023 as the reference year.
  • Illustrative soil-water modelling: Comparisons between different soil assumptions under consistent weather inputs.
  • Three hypothetical stress scenarios: Loss of irrigation supply (S1), extreme rainfall sensitivity (S2) and a prolonged dry period (S3).
  • Farmer Priority Selector: An interface allowing users to explore different priorities rather than accepting a single universal recommendation.
  • NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6: A separate Climate 2050 Lens examining daily precipitation in one simulated year under SSP2-4.5.

What makes YETOS different?

Same rain, different soil: Weather inputs remain consistent while soil assumptions change, making their influence easier to understand.

Transparent uncertainty: The application distinguishes historical NASA data, hypothetical scenarios, illustrative model outputs and conditional climate projections.

Human decision-making: The prototype supports exploration rather than imposing a single optimal decision.

Scientific traceability: Source provenance, modelling assumptions, decision registers and automated tests are documented in the public GitHub repository.

Technical implementation

The application was developed during the BUILD period of NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 using Python, Streamlit and GitHub.

It includes eight interactive sections, historical and projected precipitation visualizations, scenario comparisons and 35 passing automated tests.

Scientific limitations

Soil parameters have not been calibrated using field measurements. Modelled unretained water is an accounting proxy, not a validated runoff, erosion or flood prediction.

The Climate 2050 Lens represents one simulated year from one climate model and scenario. It does not establish a long-term climate trend or provide a weather forecast.

YETOS 2050 does not provide validated crop-yield predictions or replace professional agronomic advice.

Our vision

The project is motivated by environmental ethics and responsibility toward future generations. We want agricultural science to become easier to understand while keeping farmers in control of their decisions.

Science informs choices. Farmers decide. Future generations inherit the consequences.
